blocks.x: Yeah, it's going, so if you want to give your name first, Mr. Bigard, then... Yeah, can we get your name now? Yes. What is your name, your full name? My full name is Alexander Lewis Bigard, Jr.
And how do you... it's A-L-E-X is how you spell the nickname you told us.
A-L-E-X, correct.
And let's see, today is April the... 30th.
30th.
In the 30th, 1960. And we're at your home at 2724 St. Peter.
St. Peter. Good.
All right, fine. Well, first thing I'd like to know is when a person's born and where?

I was born in the city of New Orleans, September 25th, 1899. In what part of town were you born? Do you remember? I mean, not as you remember, but where your folks live. In the French part of town, 1726 Northville, Creole part of town.
1726 Northville, right? Northville. I see. What kind of music did you hear when you were young?

Oh, nothing else but Dixieland music. Did your father play any instrument? I know your uncle was a violin player. You liked them low about... My uncle was a violin player. My uncle was a violin player. Well, my daddy was a... He started trumpet. But he never did violin. I know. I know. Anyone else in the family that played? Of course, we know your brother. Oh, yeah. I have a wonderful brother, Bonnie Biggoin. He's the top musician. Were there any other members of the family, any other brothers or sister that played anything? No, sir. Did your mother play or sing at any instrument? No, sir. I had a cousin that played trumpet. Natty Dominic. Oh, yes. I know him very well in Chicago. Yeah, he's in Chicago. That's right. That's the only one in my family that was playing music. I decided Professor Perron, well, he's a cousin of mine. Well, he's a cousin. Cousin of mine. Biggoin. How was he related? Was he through your mother's side of the family? Through my mother's side. Can you tell us something about your uncle? What was his name? Emile Biggoin. He was a violin player. And he was playing with Sidney Desvines Orchestra. And also he played at the West End Bungalow. Was he older than your father or younger brother? No, he was younger than my father. Way younger than my father. Who was at the West End Bungalow?
They had Walter Deku on piano. Emile Biggoin on violin. And they had Bill Matthews was playing drum.

And they had Joe Howard playing trumpet. Was there a clarinet did you mention? Yes. No. No. Who was the clarinet? Who was the clarinet? Was there a clarinet did you mention? The clarinet player was uh, The clarinet player was uh, Louis Nelson. Biggoin. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Can you tell us anything about your, anything else about your uncle? Uh, when did he die about? I don't even know. No. Actually, you wouldn't know, but I just wondered if you ever talked to me about it, you know? That's right. Or what other bands he played in, if you remember? I know he played with Sidney Disney and Big Arts Orchestra. They had a band of his own. He had his own band. And he played with King Oliver and Mud Carry and Oris. That was the three bands he played in. I know Manuel Mineta talks about he used to play with your uncle, too. That's right. Did you work with your uncle much or so? Oh, yeah. I worked with him plenty.
In what bands?

With Sidney Desvines Orchestra. Can you tell us how you started in music? Your first instrument, what it was? Did you start on drums or something else? On drums. On drums. On drums. I've taken lessons with Professor Cantrell. Oh, yes. Old man, Lloyd Cantrell, was playing drums with Peter Ones Orchestra. Can you remember how you got your first set of drums, what they were like? Oh, yeah. My first job I had was over at Tom Anderson's Cabaret. I played there with Adolphe Ducanger, Albert Ducanger, and Pete Ducanger.
Were they brothers?
Yeah, they were brothers.
Oh. What instruments did they play?

Pete played clarinet. Albert played trumpet. And Adolphe, he played piano, but Adolphe got killed in an automobile accident. All right. What kind of a set of drums did you have when you started? How big a bass drum? You just showed us your bass drum. I had the same size drum that I have now, 14 by 28. And I just set a Ludwig drum. But those are not the same drums. What thing is this? That's a Ludwig. That's a Ludwig drum. Yeah. You say it has a good tone, better than most tones. Yeah, it's wonderful. It has a wonderful tone. I know it sounds good when we hear you play it. I know.
You're one of the few drummers that can seem to play a melody on the drums. You get a melody out of them, and that wasn't solo on Tiger Ray.
Oh, yeah.
Last Sunday, that was really melodic. That surprised me.

Well, by me, I guess, by me being an old-time drummer, and I practiced a lot, and I was taught the way I practiced, and the way I was taught to practice, caused me to be able to make the things that I make. Of course, it's not the modern runs of today, but those older runs, to me, sound better than the modern runs that they're making today, because lots of times, the drums break time, and they don't know what they be doing. That's right. They're just making those runs, and that's about it. But I count to my beats, and I guarantee you I'll make it on time. How much older are you than Barney? I am six years old in Barney. Six years. Yeah.
And how much older are you than Dominic? Are you about the same age as Barney?

Oh, no. Dominic is way older than me. Dominic must be about 66, 67 years old. He's 66. He could have retired last summer. He was 65 last summer, but he's still working up there. Oh, yeah. He's still working. Must be about 66 now. August the 2nd is his birthday.
Back at that Ducanje Orchestra, did they have a trombone or a bass and all that?
No, this was a full-piece combo. Wow.
Now, what was that neighborhood like around Anderson's?

Oh, it was sort of a nightclub. Was that the one on Rampart Street? That's the one that was on Rampart Street Canal in Iberville. Yeah. And another one was in the old Tenderline District there on Basin Street. Basin and Iberville. That was the relation. Is that the one they called the Annex? Did they call that the Annex? Annex. The Annex. I was wondering more about when you first started on drums. Did you have a teacher right away, an old man Contrell, or did you just pick it up first yourself? Or how come you were interested in drums? Well, I'll tell you what happened. When I was a kid, I used to always be having two faults in my hand, playing. And my daddy used to run me out the house, say, boy, you make too much noise, get out of here with that. But you hit on it. Yeah, I'd hit on the plates. On the plates. On the plates. And he told me, he says, you like that instrument? I says, yeah, daddy. He says, I'm not going to buy you no drums. He says, that's too much noise. That's too much work. Too much, you got too much of a load. So he bought me a clarinet. And he, I was supposed to take a clarinet lesson with Lorenzo Teal. Oh, yeah. But instead of me going to take my lesson on the clarinet, I used to take my clarinet, put it on each step and hide and go tell him I was taking lessons. So he comes to find out I wasn't taking lessons. Instead of going to take clarinet lessons, I was going to take drum lessons. From old man can't tell. So when he finally just left me pick up on what I like. And that's how I started playing drums.
How did you take drum lessons from him? Did you have a drum or did you use his drum?
Oh, no. We had a pad.
Oh, I see.
We had a regular drum pad.
And did you get one at the same time you had your clarinet there? Or how did you buy one?
I bought one. Yeah, I bought a pad. I did not have any drum at all. You practiced on the drum pad? On the pad. On the pad. What kind of sticks did you have?
Did you have the regular sticks at that time?
Regular drum sticks. Regular drum sticks with the pad.
Line or heavy sticks?

Light sticks. Light sticks. Do you remember anything else about your lessons? What he did? Did you have a method book or how he taught you? Oh, I have a method book. Fisher's method. Oh, Fisher. Yeah, Fisher. Is that the Otto Lange or Carl Fisher? Carl Fisher. It wasn't the Lange? No. Carl Fisher. Because I think Fisher published the Lange method too. Yeah, but at that time it was the Carl Fisher. We haven't talked to his son yet. We'll ask him more about his father too. But is there anything else you can remember about your lessons? What kind of, how he taught you? Well, he said I had a pretty good idea. Is he a strict teacher? Strict teacher. He's very strict. He's very strict. And lots of times he sent me in his place at Spanish Ford at Trencini. And he's not feeling good. He said go to my place tonight. And he'd, I guess he'd get words from Professor Pierron, how was I making out? Yeah. And Professor Pierron told him that I was one of them. Who else was in the Pierron band? At that time they had Peter Bocchage. He was playing trumpet. He had Xilophone. And they had Lorenzo Teo was playing clarinet. And they had their, Louie Warnock was playing alto sax. Steve Lewis was playing piano.
When I went. Bass player?
Oh, Steve Lewis, piano player.
No, but did you have a bass player? No.
No. Just on the last, he was using Peter Bocchage's brother on bass. The Charlie, Charlie. Charlie, Charlie, Charlie. Then he started using Charlie Bocchage on the last.
On what instrument, Charlie?
Charlie Bocchage was playing banjo.
And the bass player is Henry.

And his brother, his other brother was playing. Oh, I thought I wondered which brother. He had another brother playing bass. That's Henry, isn't it? I'm not sure. I can't think of his name. Well, we have that anyway. Yeah.
From Pete.

Can you remember anything else about your lessons? Did he ever take up the bass drum with you, or just entirely snare drums? Oh, no. He was strictly on the time. He used to make his beat all the time. One, two, three, four. One, two, three, four. Slide your foot over on two and three and up on four. Yeah, that's right. It's on the beat.
Yeah. You come down on one. One. And you slide to the left on two. Oh, that's right. Slide to the right on three and then up on four. Up on four. That's right. Good.

Oh, he was very strict. Somebody told me that he used to work at Whirline's or one of the music stores. Do you remember when you were taking lessons that he worked in their drum department, maybe repairing them or doing something? I don't know. Well, uh... Do you know? The only thing I know about it, I don't know how true it is, but they told me he used to give lessons at Whirline. Yeah. He used to give lessons at Whirline. Yeah. He used to give lessons at Whirline. Somebody told me he'd always... Any new drums would come in, he'd always inspect them and be sure they were right. That's right. I didn't know if he really worked there. He had a set of drums I've never seen before, that falling drums. Well, I heard about that once. The snare drum and bass... Everything would fall. The bass drum would fall and the snare drum would fall. They'd have it in a flat case. Yeah, I never saw. What make was that, do you know? I don't know. But I know he used to handle the best. Yeah, it must have been the fine set. The best that would do it. That would be good for a drummer. You wouldn't have to carry that big bass drum. He was a wonderful drummer. Oh, yeah.
By the way, do you regret your father's advice not taking it, you know? I mean...

Well, no. I liked it what I liked and that was it. You don't mind carrying all those drums? I don't mind carrying it. And we have it easy now because we have a lot of transportation. Definitely before. Before you had to get on the street car and you had to go to public service and get a permit. And if you wouldn't have that permit, the conductor wouldn't leave you on. Did you charge the same fare as the regular? Same regular fare, but didn't charge you no fare for your drums. Yeah. Did you ever play any parades that you had to carry your drums in the marching parades? Oh, yeah. I played the Excelsior Brass Band. Excelsior? Yeah. When was that? About how long ago? About 30 years ago. 25, 30 years ago.
That was after World War I, huh?
Yeah.
Was it before Depression? Yeah.

I think it was before Depression. Because lots of times I played funeral with them and played parade. Then when they had dance at the background, I used to play with them in the brass band at the background. And Kid Rene was upstairs in a dance hall. She used to have two bands. Kid Rene would be upstairs and the brass band would be downstairs.
Were you playing dance band work at the same time?
What? Yeah.
What dance band were you playing with when you played with the Excelsior?
I played at the May Philippe Orchestra. Who was the leader of that? Can you tell us about that? Octave Gasper. He was the leader. He was a bass player.
Before we get away from the Excelsior, who was in that band? We ought to get that.
Well, I'm telling you the fact that it would be hard for me to remember all those fellas. He was the leader. Who was the leader? Uh-huh. Na-Na Moret. He was a trumpet player.
Yes. You called him Na-Na?
We called him Na-Na. I don't know. I don't know which his voice. They called him Na-Na Moret.
Why did you call him that? That's a funny nickname.

Well, that's all we had knew. I knew him, boy. He was an old man. He was strict. Very strict. And he was the leader of the band. I knew that. Remember any other trumpets? I don't know. I couldn't remember. Any of the trombone players? Yeah, I know. Buddy Johnson was one of the trombones. Buddy Johnson was one of the trombones. I believe Peter Bocasch. They played trumpet. Yeah. Peter Bocasch. Hippolyte Shawls. Oh, yeah. I remember them. And old man Giles. You know what I'm talking about? Giles. Albert Giles. He was Albert Giles' daddy. He was playing bass drum.
Is that Clay Giles? The man they call Clay?

That's Albert Giles' daddy. I believe it's Albert Giles Sr. That's right. That's his daddy. Clay was his uncle. You're right. Yeah, because he's a junior. Yeah. Did they have alto horns or saxes? Oh, yeah. What did they use? Yeah. Alto horn. And baritone horn did they have? Yeah, baritone horn. I couldn't remember just who. How many pieces were in the band there, Albert? Huh?
About how many pieces?
Well, it was about a 12 piece. 12 to 15 pieces.
And you played the snare?
Snare drum, yeah. I played snare drum and cymbal.
Oh, yeah. How'd that work?
Well, it worked pretty good.
I mean, not at the same time.
You see, the snare drum. Mm-hmm. And when we'd be going out, I'd play the cymbal.
Oh, I see, yeah. On the bass drum?
No, I wouldn't play the bass drum. I had one ordinary man playing the bass. That was Mr. Jives.
How cool.
He was playing the bass drum. And I was playing just the snare drum and cymbal.
Where'd you hook the cymbal on?
Right on the side of the snare drum.
Right.
Yeah. See, how'd you be going now? Where are your fans? Where did you get that idea from, huh? Well, that was all...

I was asking about the band at the Lyric Theater. What kind of a band it was, what they did there? Boy, at the Lyric Theater, they had a wonderful band over there. They used to play for the shows. And they had Andrew Kimball was playing trumpet. And Margaret Kimball, his wife, was playing piano. And they had Johnny Lindsay was playing trombone. And Red Happy was playing drum. And Lurie Nelson was playing clarinet. And old man John Robichaud, he was playing violin. He was the leader? He was the leader. Did they play anything like overtures or just for the shows or different acts? Well, no. They mostly played jazz. Jazz. Jazz. Jazz. No more. They mostly played jazz. No more. Did they read any? Oh, yeah. Yeah. Did they play for the movies or any? Did they have movies in those days? Yeah, they had music. Yeah, they had music. I mean the movie, motion pictures, did they play for those? No, they didn't play for motion pictures. They played for the vortical. Just the vortical. Yeah, the vortical. Just the vortical. Did they read everything or did they just read part of it? Well, no. They read all the orchestration supposed to be wrote. But I mean lots of times they played fake numbers like the average musician does. No. But I know one thing, they had really a good orchestra and not only that. They had a man behind them, Professor Robichaud. He was wonderful. Because that was, that was, I played with him when he died, way before he died. I played about five years with him. And he'd make us come to rehearsal tonight and we got a job for tomorrow night. He wouldn't bring the same kind of music we played that day. He brought some other kind of music. And when he put it before, he said, what? We ain't seen it before. He said, what? You called yourself a musician? Well, we gonna play that tonight. What he rehearsed, he wouldn't play it on the job the next night. He'd bring something else. He'd say, yeah, you call yourself a musician? Play that night. Oh, there at the Lyric, did you play, did they play in a pit or did they ever play a number? Yeah, a pit. Did they ever play up on the stage too for special numbers or anything? No, no. They played in a pit. How big a place was that theater? That's torn down. I never did see that. Well, the theater was about, about bigger. That house on the end of this, this house on the end. I wondered how many, would it seat a couple of thousand you think maybe or something? About 1,500 people. 1,500 maybe? Yeah, about 1,500 people. Was that all colored? That was just far colored? All colored. All colored. Sure. That's where Bessie Smith and, uh, I couldn't tell you about it. Mamie Smith, Bessie Smith, all those girls used to come down there. Yeah. Did you ever play in that band? Yeah. At the theater too? Yeah, I played in the same theater. I was busy. Sorry, we can stop in. Sorry. Well, we were talking about the Lyric Theater. Yeah. How late did that run? Do you know when that closed down? Well, about, uh, 10.30. 9.30, 10.30. No, I meant though in years. Well, you mean the band or what? No, the whole theater. How long did the, how late did that last? Did they tear it down or burn down or what happened to it? I never did know. They tore it down. Tore it down. Yeah, tore it down. When was that? During the Depression about or when do you know? Oh yeah, it was, yeah, yeah, it was before Depression. Before Depression. Before Depression. Before Depression. Did you play Midnight Rambles there? Oh yeah, I played with John Robichaud over there. Yeah, I played with, I played with the band himself. And you played Midnight Rambles, huh? Yeah, yeah. How did that work? Well, you see, after the show, then they had what they call a ramble. In other words, a Midnight Rambles is just like everybody gathering in a place. No playing out. And they're like a jubilee or something like that. Yeah. That's what they were. Late, huh? Yeah. After the show. After the show. Now, lots of times we'd have jobs. After the show we'd go play over at the La Luziana restaurant. Oh yeah. John Robichaud used to have all that kind of way. Used to have all that. Would that be a special dinner, banquet or something? Yeah. A special dance. Dance? Yeah, a special dance.
Well, Harrison Bones told us about that. Remember? He said he'd go over there.
Yeah, Harrison Bones played with us.
At that same time you were there, huh?
But he was playing the theater when I was there. No, he played with the orchestra. Before? Yeah.
Yeah. Who was in the band when you were there?

Well, with John Robichaud's band they had Willie Paggio. He was playing trumpet. Harrison Bones was playing trombone. Moistad Garner was playing piano. Moistad Garner was playing piano. Old Man Kimball, Kimball's daddy, was playing bass. Willie San Diego was playing banjo. Professor Robichaud was playing violin. And I was playing drums. Clarinet? Did you name him a clarinet? I'm trying to remember. Clarinet? Well, we had old man Charlie McCurdy. He was playing clarinet and sax. What's sax?
He played tenor.
Then sometimes we'd have old man Sam Dutre playing with us. Sam Dutre's daddy, the one that played tenor. Did he play tenor or clarinet any time too? No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.

No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. often in Chicago. I lived up there and every time Louis Armstrong come to town with Natty Dominick, I knew very well. We'd go up to see Barney at the theater and he told us a little bit about T.O. too, how he studied with T.O. and I noticed that Barney uses both lips on the cupboard over his teeth and not very many people here do that anymore. Do you know that the T.O.s ever teach him that? I forget. I don't know if he told me if T.O. taught him. Well, I'll tell you, it was not T.O. that taught him the clarinet and the way of speaking. T.O.'s grandfather is the one that taught him. Was that Papa or Louis? Papa T.O. Papa T.O. and after Papa T.O. taking and he told Barney, he says, Barney, I can't teach you anymore. He says, you know as much as me. He said, but go to Lorenzo and he's finished teaching. When Barney went back to Lorenzo, Lorenzo told Barney, there's nothing I can't do for you, you know as much as me. All you can do is go for yourself. Did Barney play sax down here more than clarinet? I thought he started more on sax. Barney was playing a C melody saxophone. A C melody. That's right. And every job that Barney would get, all the best of clarinet players when they'd be out of a job, well they knew Barney was a weak man because he couldn't execute the clarinet like those guys was doing. So naturally they would go up there and see the man, whoever was the leader of the band, and he'd leave Barney go. Barney would come home, well I was single then. Barney would come home crying. So he said, mama, he said, well they called him Lorenzo, but they used to call him Big, they called him Big Eye Lou. He said, Big Eye Lou took my job. My grandma, my grandma, one reason one day because my mother, she died of childbirth, but he called my grandmother Mama. So she said, well why don't you give up? He said, no mama, I have to tell him. He said, I want to learn how to play the clarinet. So he'd go and get another job. My mother would be all bump. He'd come home crying. He says, my grandmother said, what's the matter now? He said, Piku took my job. My grandmother said, Barney, why don't you get yourself a job and go to work in the day? Give up. He says, no mother. He says, I'm deterrent. I'm deterrent. So he fooled around, he fooled around, he got another job. He was playing with Amos White. So finally, I know him twice. You heard him talk about that. Yes. He gets a job at Tom Anderson. And he had, he had, he had, she, Barbaran was playing the drum with her. He had Barney on tenor, C Melody at that time. And he had, Albert Nicholas was down here at that time. He had Albert Nicholas. And he had Udell on piano from St. Louis. And he had Willie Santiago on banjo. So, Barney told Arnold, he says, you know Arnold, he says, every time I get a job, he says, they take me, they turn around, they fire me and they take one of them stars. So Arnold said, well, you don't worry about it. He says, we're going to work a plan that you're going to be here. Well, I know I knew that Barney was a good musician, but he couldn't execute the clarinet like these other guys was doing around there. So Albert Nicholas was a fine clarinet player. So Albert and Barney, they got together and they made an arrangement that they would take and teach one another about the instrument. So Albert was never much of a reader, but Barney was the number one musician. So Barney said, well, Albert said, I'll tell you what I'll do with you. He said, if you learn me how to affect this clarinet, he says, I'll learn you the music. Well, they decided. Every day, I was working at the West End Bungalow at that time, and I used to sleep in the band there. I said, oh, for God's sake, get out of here with all that noise. And my grandmother said, well, he's got to learn, he's got to learn, he's got to learn. Yeah, he's got to learn. I said, well, wake me up. Let him go in the yard and play. And so finally they got together and they did turn out to be the best sacks team that they had around the city of New Orleans. And Barney then improved so much on that clarinet, he was getting great. So then Sidney Deadbeam was playing on the boat then, stealing a captain. Sidney tried to get them. He wanted the two of them. Well, though they wouldn't go. So T-Bob Barbran gets telegram from King Alba. King Alba wanted him to get some musicians from down there. So he got Alba Nicholas, he got Barney, Barney and him and they went to Chicago. Well, they joined King Alba's band up in Chicago. So when they joined King Alba's band in Chicago, Barney stood with them a long time. Then Duke Gelton drove over. And that's where Barney made a success. So when Barney came down here with Duke Gelton, first time Duke was down here, he had gave Duke a two weeks notice that he was leaving. So Big Alba and Pete Kool and fellas that was up there around the bandstand, giving Barney plenty of compliments the way he played clarinet. So Barney said, now look, he said, you know, y'all made me cry plenty. He said, y'all really made me cry. He says, now, he said, y'all got an opportunity. He says, Duke Gelton's down here right now. He needs a clarinet player. He said, yeah, want one of y'all up there, give him an audition. Probably take one of y'all. No, indeed, Barney, we ain't going behind you. No, indeed. He said, well, I'm sorry. He says, Duke got a two weeks notice. He said, now, if you want a job, he says, go up there, Duke, make an audition with Duke and Duke probably will hire. But they never, never do it. I was going to ask a little more about the violin player since you knew your uncle, of course, very well. How did he play? What kind of a part did they play? Oh, Monk, he was a good musician. He was a great musician. In fact, I think Monk was a better violin player than Pierron. But Pierron just had the name amongst the public. But to my estimation, he was better than Pierron. How was the old man Robichaud on violin? He was a- Well, he was never much of a violin player. But I tell you, he was a good musician. Good arranger and all. Yeah, good arranger. But he was never, I mean, it looked like you couldn't get no tone out of a violin like these other guys, you know. But uh, as far as arranging, as far as you, you the music. I don't care how many men you could have playing, you give everybody a part. You could tell what the man's not playing his part, what he's not making right, what he's making right, what he's not making right. He was a good director, a good musician, but he was never, not much of a violin player. Well, would he write out those arrangements himself? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. You could hum a song and he, and he'd write it. Oh, he was great. He was great, but he was not much of a violin player. Couldn't execute it faster. Yeah. But he was wonderful. I'm wondering in the, say, the old time Dixieland type of music, you know, when they just fake, what kind of a part would the violin play? Would he stick right to the lead to playing like the trumpet part, or what did he do? Oh no, he'd fake it now, he'd fake it now. Would he play variations? Variations. Something like the clarinet, like a clarinet. Chords and all up and down. And it would sound good. It would sound real good. Would they harmonize with any other songs? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah, they would harmonize. Did he sometimes play a second part like down low maybe two or what? That's right. See, I never heard violin much. I heard Peter Boccage play the other night though. Yeah. On violin, he did very well too. Yeah. But I never heard much of the old time. How did he do it? And I'll tell you, sounds pretty good. Well, I'll tell you, in fact, not to say knocking, but the average band that we have around is not playing Dixieland music. No, that's right. Not like the old time, I bet. No, that's right. They're not playing. They're playing jazz. You see, Dixieland music can not be played fast, fast, fast, and see those guys playing some of these numbers. They got a swinging tempo. Two beats of them else, you see. Now, there you go. That, of course, that's the way you got to play with them today. They want you to do that. But that is supposed to be one beat. Dixieland is a one beat. Dixieland beat is not no two beat, but that's the way they want you to play today. You got to play the way they want you to play. Dixieland music is not no, there's not no 4-4-3. When did they start putting the 4-4 in? Oh, this year. Long time. Well, the original. The only time that we played 4-4 is when we was going out. See, like I tried explaining the fightless cymbal and the snare drum together. That's the only time we played a 4-4 when we were going out. But today, they want you to play a 4-4 beat all the way through.
Well, the brass bands do what you're talking about. They play 2-4 until the out chorus. Now, you hear them do that.
What's that?
The brass bands will play 2-4 until the out chorus, you know. Then they'll double.

Then they'll double. It's like you're talking about. It's like I'm talking about. Well, that's the way the orchestra used to play. But they don't play like that now. And they didn't play nothing. I didn't know that guy definitely swing all together than what these guys had years ago. They were playing with a song.
What did you call that music in those days? That was Dixieland. You called it Dixieland then? That was Dixieland.

I think the music today is... They haven't got the real idea of Dixieland. And it's hard for you to get a man to form up a band with Dixieland music. Simple fact, this guy says he knows this and he knows that. And when it comes to flying, he don't know nothing. Yeah. He's got his ideas. What did they call the old time bands? Somebody told me they used to call them ragtime bands quite a bit. Yeah. Did you make any difference between the word like ragtime or Dixieland or jazz? Or when did those different words start to be used? Well... Can you remember that? The ragtime band is just like you take most of what we used to call, I don't know, ragtime band is just like in all of a summer player number right now. So I'll take Mac to life. You know... Da da da da... Da da da da... Like that. But we didn't play like that. See Dixieland. Da da da da da... Da da da da... Da da da da da... Da da da da... See you ain't killing nobody. But... Da da da da... Da da da da... That's right time. That's right time music. That ain't no Dixieland music. That's a different beat altogether. I mean you're not uh... You're not got your harmony falling there just right. Not to my estimation. I might be wrong.
What did you say that fast time is? What do you call that fast time again?
That's that fourth rhythm.
Yeah. I mean do you give it any special name? That's not Dixieland.
Not to my... Not to my...
What would you call it?
I call it ragtime music like that.
Oh that's ragtime.
You call it ragtime. That's what you call it ragtime music. But Dixieland music... Da da da da... Da da da da... Da da da da... See what do you call it? Da da da da da... Da da da da...
That's ragtime music. That's two different kinds of beats right there. Well that's slower music. I imagine it would be better to dance to, would it not, Allie?

Well yeah, it's better to dance with Ant and you, and the man gonna harmonize, gonna make this part just right. In other words he doesn't have to do it. See now we played, we used to play Tiger Rag, not like they play, we played da da da da da da da da da. See? That was Dixieland. Da da da da da da da da da da. Da da da da da da da da. Da da da da da. Give a man a chance to make these parts, gonna make it right. When you do that right time music, that's two different kinds of music all together. Not to say you can't play it. You can play it. You understand? But you're not giving, you're not giving the right tempo to that number. You don't get the same interpretation. That's right. That's the same interpretation. Because a man make anything in a fast number, you know that. Yeah.
Anything.
Then it's gonna sound good. But when you put that beautiful man, he's just planning up, if you read that part right, he's got plenty to cut, don't you worry about that.
Yeah, yeah, that's right.
That's where the average band is playing around here. But they're not playing, that's what I said, they're not playing the real Dixieland music.

Now I say the Ducanger band, what would they play that you were with? Oh, they played Dixieland music. They were very common. They were fakers strictly or were they reading too? No, no, no, they're music.
And they'd fake after that.

They'd play the first parts and then after that they'd go for the cell. Well, what kind of arrangements did they have? Did they have stock arrangements or did they have the regular orchestra arrangements?
Oh, regular orchestra arrangements.
They make them themselves? No, no. They bought them, huh? Yeah. They bought them. Now, what do you call jazz music? How would you demonstrate jazz tempo?

That's in order of speaking about it just a while ago. Fast. Yeah. Do you know when that word began being used around here in connection with the bands, when they started calling them jazz bands? About what year? Was it before the war, after the First World War? When was it, do you know? I think it was after the First World War. I think it was after the First World War. Yeah, after the First World War. Because that, before then, it left a dish around here. Well, to change the subject again, I'd like to get back to your family again, to your uncle. Do you remember how old he was when he died? He was 49 years old. Only 49. That wasn't old at all, was it? 49. I always think of him as an old man, you know, because it was so long ago. 49 years old. But he wasn't old. 49 years old. He died from a penny. Acute of penny. And he never said who he took lessons from, or where he got his start, or... I believe, if I'm not mistaken, I believe Professor Shelley Nee, I believe. Oh yeah. I'm not mistaken. No thanks. Can I borrow your ice cream? Yeah, look, that one over there. All right. You can give him one of those. Let me stop right here. Or one of the, did he ever say which was the first band he played in, or any other... Well, to my... I think he started playing at the... he worked at West End Bungalow, Goodwild. Then he left out there and he formed a band with Sid and Dead Green. He used to call it Dead Green Orchestra and Big Art. I just wonder if there's any other band even before your time that he talked about that you didn't even know. And he worked with Kid Orrish and Mudcarrier. And he worked with King Arthur. Mm-hmm. Dead Green, King Arthur. That's the most band that I know he worked with. Sid and Dead Green, King Arthur and Kid Orrish. I think that I haven't seen Barney for several years now since I moved here. About six, it's been almost five years ago. And I think he told me then, you say that was his grandmother that raised him. That's right. But she's still living at that time. I don't know, she died at the age of 96. She died three years ago. Three years, that's what I wonder. Because five years ago she was still living. Yeah. Three years ago. I wondered if she was still living. She's not living. Yeah. Any other of your relatives? Your father, of course, has been gone, I guess, a long time. Some of my father did. Does Barney ever get back here? In the last year in California, I tried to find him, Professor Minetta and I went out there. And he wasn't in Los Angeles, I think. I think he'd been out of town. He was going to open a little chicken farm. Did he ever do that? I don't know. He's with Louie in there. But he went back with Louie, I know. He's back with Louie, yeah. Because I got a letter from him about a month and a half ago. They told me that thing was getting tight around California, that Louie wanted to come back and he was going back with Louie. So now they're on the road, I know it, because I didn't get any letter from him. We'll get to see him. We've never interviewed him for Tulane either. I was hoping we'll see him some of these days. Of course, Louie won't come down here right now, but someday we'll see him. Oh, I guess. I guess Louie will be peeping down here pretty soon. I guess so. He might come for a visit. Yeah. When was the last time Barney was back home? Well, Barney's been back home about three years now. About three years. He was down here with Louie the last time he was there. Have you played together recently, Alec?
You and Barney? No. You haven't played together in a while.

Well, I'm the one who got Barney East Stark. Oh yeah? How did that work? Well, Barney wasn't playing with nobody. And I got him with a little band used to rehearse by the St. Bernard Market. Oh man Bernard Orchestra. And I got Barney in that little band. I'm the one who started him out. Then Barney played with me a while with the Maple Leaf Band. I'm the one who started him out.
Who was in Oh Man Bernard's orchestra?

I know Adolf Rooney was a drummer. Paul Muglia was playing. I remember playing trumpet or something like that. I know Paul Muglia used to play trumpet. But no, I was Paul Muglia. I couldn't remember. What was Bernard's name? Did you know? No, I knew Bernard. He was a trumpet player. Oh Man Bernard. Oh Man. Oh Man Bernard.
Oh Man Bernard.
Oh Man Bernard. Oh M-E-R. Oh Man Bernard.
Oh, back to De Conge. What happened after you left De Conge's orchestra?

Those brothers? Well Pete, he went to, uh, Pete's supposed to be in Europe right now. And Albert, it was the last time I heard he was at St. Louis. But I heard he had given up playing music. He was a policeman up there. And Adolf Rooney got killed in an automobile accident. Come from playing.

No, I mean who'd you join after you left then? Who did I join? Mm-hmm. It's his buddy there. Huh? It's his buddy there, I believe, huh? Buddy Petit. Yeah. I went and started playing with Buddy Petit. Buddy Petit's band. How long did you play with Buddy Petit, Allie? About three years.
About three years? Mm-hmm. And how was his band? Who was in his band at that time?
Well at that time he had, well I've been playing with Buddy Petit. He had a fella by the name of George Washington was playing trombone.
He had Buddy Matty was playing banjo. Little Chester was playing bass. And Little Pills was playing clarinet.
Pills, did he have any name? What was his real name?

I don't know. I don't know. We used to call him Cripple Pills. Quacko was his name. Huh? Quacko. Quacko, I don't know. Well anyway, that's the part I could remember. We used to call him Pills, you know. He had a good band.
He had a good band, didn't he?

Everybody was crazy about Buddy Petit. Uh-huh. Buddy Petit could take nine jobs in one night. And he couldn't play but one. And everybody was looking for Buddy Petit. He'd go to the dance, don't see Buddy, everybody leave the dance, go where Buddy's at.
Well he must have been a fine cornet player, trumpet player.
Well he wasn't that exact, but I mean when he played, he played. Uh-huh.
Did he play trumpet or cornet then?
He played uh, cornet.
Cornet.

Yeah, played cornet. Was he a hard worker or did he? Oh he was a hard worker. He was a hard drinker too. Yeah, he, he, he. Where did he live then, those days when you played? Those days he was living on Durbanie, between St. Anthony and Poggle.
A guy like Buddy, would he play the whole tune or would he take down or what?

Well I tell you, the number that Buddy used to play with, lots of these trumpet players around here couldn't play. Now I don't know how he played. He used to play what we called Scott Joplin number. The Red Bulls, we called it the Red Bulls. But all things like that. And that's what you used to get, the people used to be crazy about what they kind of knew during that time.
Uh-huh. Did he, did he read those books or did he just have-
Well, not to mind knowing, he didn't read, but I know he got them. How you got them, he got them.
Well, did anybody in the band, I mean, were any of those members that you mentioned, were they readers at all? Not that I know of.

Never used the arrangements then, never had the music there for any of those. They let him just play what they, what they thought went, did it sound good? And he had the biggest reputation around here, and then the trumpet player. And then another one had a big reputation around here, Kid René. Kid René had a bigger reputation than Louis Armstrong. Just say he didn't want to go away from him, he had the best opportunity of his life. They're begging him, come to Chicago. King Alba wanted to send him to him. He said to go. They used to call him the little Turk. And when we'd, uh, that time we used to advertise the truck, you know, like I said, for a dance going on, you might catch about three or four bands that's out on the streets, for different places giving dances. And when they tell you little Turk's at the next corner, they could be going that way, they wouldn't go that way, they'd go around the corner. It's like, like a dog, your friend, play the past, play the bulldog on by them. So, let's keep out the way. That was a kick. That was good days, those days.
Well, uh, when you played on the trucks like everybody petite, uh, what kind of a drum set did you have at that time, alright?
Record drum set.
Uh, uh, did you have, uh, you'd have the foot pedal then, would you say?
Overhead foot pedal.
Overhead. You had the overhead, uh? Overhead foot pedal. Oh, you had the same sort of arrangement that you were describing, don't you?

That's right. You see, we didn't have no big tum tum or nothing like that. We just had them little bit of tum tum on the side of a wood block and one cymbal, and that overhead pedal. And you'd snag drum, and you'd stand, that's it.
And you'd put that all on the truck? Oh yeah. Whereabouts on the truck would you sit, Alan?
The first. First. First. First. Thank you.

The drummer would be right up near the driver then, the front end of the truck? Yes. The bass player would be on the end. Back at the tailgate. Yeah, tailgate. Him and the tri-roll. I was going to ask. Some more about Buddy Petit. The other night we talked to Sammy Penn, the drummer who used to play with him too. He talked like Buddy lived across the lake at the end of his life. Do you remember those days? Did he ever talk about going across the lake much? Buddy did go across the lake. He lost his health. That's where he lost his health. He went to TB. I didn't know he had TB. And he died. He looked pretty small anyway, didn't he? He died across the lake. He died over there then. Did any of his old man Joe Petit, I knew the trombonist, his stepfather, he never lived over there though, did he? No. I thought maybe Buddy, Sammy talked like his family lived over there or something. I didn't know what he meant though, by his family. Did he have a wife over there maybe or something? Do you know? I don't know. I couldn't tell you whether he went to live over there after that. You weren't with him in those days. You never worked across the lake then with him? Oh yeah, I went across the lake with him. Not there. I used to go to Pugaloosa. Just there wasn't a job though. You didn't go over there like all summer to stay there. Oh no, no, no, no, no, no, no. That's what I wondered. Just jobs.
Yeah. I was wondering about him now. I was asking you before. Could he stay out for a whole mamba and keep punching on him? Oh yeah, yeah. He was that strong, huh? That's right. That's right.

But not loud, they say. No, he wasn't quite loud, but he was pretty good. He was pretty good. Now what about other trumpet players there around the time you were playing with Buddy? Would they play a whole mamba or would they take it down? Oh yeah, you'd take like this little fella there, Kid René, when I was telling you about it. He was about one of the best trumpet players around there to my estimation. He would only take one course, he'd take two chords. He'd take it above the staff. And stay above the staff. You ain't never heard nobody play high society above the staff. He'd take two steps to stay there. He's one of your little greatest there around here. He'd play with me until he died. We worked at the Brown Derby on Canal Street.
Well I was there, I heard you. You heard me? Yeah, I think I was in the Navy then, or maybe I was on vacation.
At the Brown Derby.
Yeah, and Morgan was there. Morgan was there. And Black Benny Turner. That's right, that's right. And I went down to see Big Eye at Lutchen's, I remember that. Yeah, that's right.

And you played Royal Garden Blues and Sister Kate. That's right. I can remember that. But then he was a sick man during the time you'd say anything, he was a sick man. But he made it on those last courses.
Oh yeah. He could give out. Much better than his records. Oh yeah. You ever heard his records? No. He was playing in the middle right just to play straight lead practically, huh Bill?

Doesn't really get cut loose, you know. He was tough. He was tough. When he was in his prime, and these bands would be out here on these advertising, and they'd tell you a little turk, we used to call them little turk, you see a little turk at the next corner, they'd support the passing block, they'd make a round of blood. Because the bands used to stay there and buck for another hour. An hour and a half. Just like you're playing for a dance. Yeah. So one would make up their mind and go.
Well now, when you were bucking each other, would you be listening to the other bands drummer? And like you were saying, listening for something he was making and try to make it?

Or anything like that? Well no, no. I never tried to imitate anyone. I always had my own ideas. I never believed in that. I make what I think I can make, and what I think I can't make, I don't try to make it. Only one I was coming up, I used to go around, these fellas I know it was better than me, and I used to catch the others and see what they'd do, and I'd come and hope I'm home. We got there and started practicing until I get what I'm on again.
Well in other words, you didn't try to out-drum each other.
No, no. You just tried to? But lots of times when we'd be playing those cameras like that, we'd be bucking against enough.
But in other words, you were just trying to help the band along, you weren't trying to get out of the band. That's right. I was drunk, drunk while wearing.

But I tell you, I was tough in my days. I was plenty tough in my days. Anybody tell you about me. I was plenty tough. I was plenty tough. I was plenty tough. Which, I'm old now, but I don't worry about none of them. You get around all right. I don't worry about none of them. You're all right, yeah. Ain't a place I ever played if I can't go back and play or if they don't want me to come back and see about a job.
Yeah. Well after you left Buddy Petite, did you go right away to Kid Renee's band? No, no, no.
After I left Buddy Petite, I worked with Sidney Desweeney. I see. Yeah. I worked with Sidney Desweeney about two years.
And who was in the band at that time with you?

At that time, I was with Sidney Desweeney, Buddy Johnson playing trombone. Sidney Desweeney playing trumpet. My uncle, he was playing violin. Willie Santiago playing banjo. And they had clarinet. Let's see what on clarinet. Sidney Desweeney was playing clarinet. And uh, Kimball was playing bass. Old man Kimball was playing bass.
Did you ever go on any trips with that band out of town or did you stay just in town?
No, we played just in town. No, the band most I went away with, it was a Maple Leaf band. I worked with them.
And you were with him about two years?

With Sidney Desweeney, yeah, two years. You never worked on the boat then any place? On the excursion boat, you never worked on any boat? Oh yeah, I worked on Steamer Capital. With who? With the Maple Leaf band. Oh, with the Maple Leaf band. Yeah.
What kind of band was Sidney Desweeney's?
Would you call that a Dixieland band or a Reedin band or both? Well, it was a Reedin band. It was an orchestra. It was an orchestra.
Now, did you get drum parts to play with that?

Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, you see it's different with orchestra than with the little bands that you're affiliated with. Because this is the reason why I say I can play all the folks with any kind of type of drumming because I play with them all. I play with fellas that couldn't read and I play with fellas that were musicians. And I play with the best of musicians that you have that's gone and some that's here today. I was going to ask a little bit more about your lessons in the beginning. How often did you take a lesson from Louis Cantrell? Twice a week. Twice a week. How long did those lessons last about? Well, it lasted about an hour. And do you remember what he charged you in those days? Fifty cents. Fifty cents a lesson. That's right. And how much did he expect you to practice every day? How long did you practice? Well, you had to practice. He used to tell me to practice two hours every day. Two hours a day. Yeah. And we had a regular pad. It was a drum, like a little drum, in the middle. It was hard. Yes. Yes, I know those little pads. Yeah. And sticks. Regular sticks. Did they have any bands in the schools in those days? What school did you go to? Did you go to a Catholic school or a public school or anything? I went to public school, but they didn't have any bands when they were done. No school bands at all. No school bands at all. No school bands at all.
Yeah. How long did you go to him for lessons about that? Two years. Two years. And how long was it before he let you play with the regular drum? Not just the drum?
Well, I'll tell you. He didn't want to get on the drums right away. I believe it was about nine months.
About nine months. Yeah.

Before he actually got to the drum. Then... What mostly he kept me on, it was most of the rolls. Oh, I see. You know. You take a lot of these drums and you get around the city today, they make your roll. Oh, no. You can't handle sticks.
Well, when you first got a drum, it was the regular snare drum, was it? Yeah. About how long?
In other words, I got the whole set of drum when I got a drum.
Oh, you did get a whole set? The whole set. And then you were working out with the bass drum, I understand, I'm sure.

Yeah. Did he ever give any lessons about how to use your foot on the pedal or anything? No, no. He just kept it with that time. Kept it with the time. I mean, with the pedal though, he didn't show anything about the pedal or cymbals or anything. Didn't talk about that. You had to catch that yourself. Yeah. Stuck to the snare drum is all he taught. Only when an orchestra wrote, you know, you had to hit a cymbal or you got a break or what you got to do, all that, things like that.
Did he give you any exercises, like wrist exercises or anything to do? Anything to loosen up your wrists?
No, no. All the movement would come in was the rolls. That's where you kept it most on the roll there. That's where you get to loosen your wrists.
Did it make you move your hand around like that?

No. No, it took your sticks. Just roll. Just roll? Just drop one stick. You see, roll is supposed to start with your left, man. Not your right. You like to jump the pick and roll the start with your right. The left hand. You just drop your stick on the pedal. Boom, boom. And you make it go fast. And speed it up. The first thing you know you're rolling. Yeah. That's the way you should do. Did Mr. Contrell ever play with you or show you with the sticks himself how to do the things? He never had a drum there at all, just on the pads or something. Did he always demonstrate it for you or before you'd do it or what did he show you? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. He'd show you just what he wants you to do. You have to, and he'd watch you. He'd make you take out your method and go give you this lesson when you had to come back with that lesson. Yeah.
You say he was very strict. In what way was he strict, Ali?

Well, I mean if he gave you a lesson you better come and tell him that you don't know that lesson because he's going to show you just how it goes. And he'll show you just how to make it. And if you come to him and you tell him how you can make this, how you make that man, give the sand.
Yeah, he's all yeah. Yeah. I suppose when you came to him and you hadn't practiced your lesson, what would he do?

Well, he wouldn't do you anything if this youth was out of half a dollar, that's all. He's all he's making the money, he didn't care, but I mean he'd punish you and tell you, well I'm going to give you two lessons for one. He'd give you that lesson over again and give you another lesson. He'd say, now you bring those two lessons to me. He was a really wonderful, wonderful teacher. I'll tell you another one that taught me plenty too, Professor Manmanetta. Oh yeah. When did you work with him? Well, I went away with him. He worked, we worked together with the Maple Leaf band. He was in the Maple? Yeah. And I left the Maple Leaf band and we were supposed to get a job in Havana, Cuba. So I quits the Maple Leaf band and gets me a job to work on United Fruit Ship. I went to go to Havana and see Miss Anna Keller. Anna Keller, yeah. Anna Keller was her name. And I got over there, I was a little too late for the job. She had got an officer from New York. Well I had to make the whole trip. It was 17 years when I came back. So the first was waiting for me. I had to go, how you been on? I said, man. Well I didn't get the job, that was all. So a little barber ran, a little lawyer barber ran was playing with my place until I come back. At that time we had dates on top of dates. We used to have to carry a book, a memo pad. And sometimes we had two jobs in a day. We'd be going every night. And little barber ran was mad to see that I came back so early. Because we was making so much money with the band. So anyway, when I came back, I went back to the band. The president gets him a job to go teach a band in Appalooza. So they needed a drummer. So he asked where I go. So I told him, yeah, I said, I'm here to go take a rest. I'm here to take a rest. We went to Appalooza, we played with the Martell Band out there. Him and I. And we were still out there three months. So we made a success when we came back.

When you played with that band, were they playing the same type of music that you'd been playing in New Orleans? I mean the same type of music? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Was it a reading band? Yeah, it was all readings.

In other words, it was a family band. Oh I see. Was that the band that Fess told us about? I believe Joe Dairnsberg, some of his folks. Martell. Was the Martell from the Appalooza? Was Joe Dairnsberg any relation or something? You remember the boy that plays Clarence in the Dory? Yeah, I believe his relation to him. He might have been around the house or something like that. Fess told us about him. He might have married one of the daughters or something. Yeah, I believe he married the daughter of that family. That was it.
Who was in the band? What were the Martell's names?

I know he had a son by the name of David Martell. He was playing trombone. And the daughter was playing banjo, Hillary, Hillary Martell. She was playing banjo and the other son was named Chester. He was playing bass. And the father? And the father was playing violin. He had another son who was playing trumpet. I just forgot his name. I can't think about his name. Professor Mineta was playing sax and I was playing drum. And we used to go to different little places like Vell Platt, little country town. Everything like that. He worked every night.
And you say it was in that band that you learned a lot from Professor Mineta?
Oh yeah, well he taught me a lot. He taught me a lot.
What, what, what, can you think of any sort of particular thing that your memory taught you?
Well, no. Sometime I, I, I, I, I, I would run across some little difficult parts of music. Oh, I see. And he would give me an idea and I'd go. And, uh, that's why I consider learning a lot.

Uh, uh, when Professor Mineta, uh, when you ever worked with Professor Mineta, uh, did you find that, uh, he, he sort of, uh, he was playing piano, did you say in that band? Oh, saxophone. Sax. Uh, did you find that he sort of led the band or, uh, or just played his part or? Oh, he was the leader of the band.
He was the leader. In other words, the old man, the violin was supposed to be the leader but Professor was
the, was the leader. Did, uh, Professor usually, uh, start the band and knock the band off? What's that? Did he usually start the band? Oh yeah, he start the band.

He started the band. Stomp off. In the old days, the violin player would always stomp off for the? Yeah, the violin player was the leader. That's right. But after we went out there and Fess took over the band, well, he made Fess be the leader. Yeah. Uh, cause I, I, I don't think that they knew about our town for it or just. Yeah, sure. I was gonna ask, I keep going back to your uncle again, uh, did he have some trade? I remember Bunk Johnson used to talk about, Bunk used to go to his house and rehearse. Where did he live? And what was his trade in the daytime? My uncle was a seagull maker. Oh, that's right. He didn't work anywhere. We had a little buckeye shop at the house. In other words, we used to call that buckeye shop because it had, we used to have six, seven people working for us. Seagull maker. Yeah. Did your father and your uncle live together then or, uh, was it all the same home? All the same home. That's our own home. Yeah. So that's the same address you gave us before on Villery Street or someplace along? 1726 North Villery. Mm-hmm. And, uh, well, the house, the house was here now since my grandmother died. It's a community problem. We had about two problems to be sold. Mm-hmm.
What band was that that Bunk was in, was it? Um, I don't know.

Bunk used to say he'd go there, like, maybe on Sunday afternoons or sometime in practice. I think the way they talk, a lot of times the, uh, musicians, if they didn't have a job, they'd get together on Sunday afternoons and practice anyway. Is that true? Yeah. Yeah. Bunked on the band. Even if they didn't have a job on a certain band, they'd just come there and rehearse. Yeah. That's right. It's called a rehearsal.
Yeah. Did you used to, do you remember them playing then? Yeah, I remember them.
Mm-hmm.
Did you ever sit in with them? Oh, no, I wasn't, I was not playing music then.

Oh, I see. I was a kid. Oh, I didn't hear that. I know Bunk, when he saw Barney in San Francisco, that was 15 years ago, he said to Barney, you won't remember me, but I remember you. And I used to go to your uncle's house. Okay, yeah. He played violin. He told Barney all about his family more than Barney could remember, he said. That's right. And he said he remembers Barney being a little kid playing around there, but Barney wouldn't remember Bunk. I was a kid too, and I used to admire when my uncle would have rehearsals. And I used to admire being a drummer. And I used to stand by the drummer, there's a Watson drummer, there's a Watson drummer, a Watson drummer. Do you know who they were? I said one day I'd be like that, Henry Martin was playing the drum with the, with Kid Ores and there. Yeah. And I used to admire where Henry Martin played.
