And I ain't never broke a head. I've heard of people that right there.
And Lady Bailey says that he never broke a drum head. Huh? Lady Bailey says he never broke a drum head.
Well, I'll tell you, I ain't never broke a drum head. I said those are the same.
And I ain't never broke down on that.

And I won't show you. And I had never said before that I hadn't broke down on that. But the man I have to take a lesson from, I said Cantrell, he told me don't never take and tighten the drum head and untighten.
Oh.
If you tighten it to a certain tune, let it stay like that.
Let it stay like that. I don't tighten my snare drum.
I don't tighten my bass drum. If I finally got my tune that I like, I put my light on. Them globes I got, they'll bring it up. What have you got in there?
Just one globe on it? No, I have about six globes.
Six globes?
What, all the way around the inside?
Yeah, and they reflect. Hold on, get on. Hold on, go. Oh, you have a little... I got it, I got even better light in my, uh... My snare drum. What do you have?
And you snare them too.
Oh, that's what I wonder about your snare drum, how you keep it up the pitch.

Oh, that's a red there, so there's a red reflector in there, or is it a red bulb? Yeah, you see? Oh, yeah. Oh, what happens, what happens there? Another bulb comes on, huh? And a blue one? They're a different colored bulb. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, they keep flashing on and off. Grim is in the color. Did you put those in there yourself, Ollie? I did.
There. Uh-huh. And that keeps the head tight. Tight.

Uh-huh. You say once you tune it up you don't bother touching it again? No, I don't. What do you tune it up to, Ollie? Well, according to that, that's supposed to be B. Oh, that's according to B, I guess on the bass pedal? Yeah, bass pedal. Uh-huh. And you just leave it like that? That's all. I don't ever tighten, I don't ever un-tighten. If it rain on it, I'll take the rag and wipe it off good and that's it. Yeah. Wow. That's good. Wow. That's good. That's good. Well, once you tune it up you don't bother touching it again? I don't. What do you tune it up to, Ollie? Well, according to that, that's supposed to be B. Oh, that's called to be B, I guess on the bass pedal? Yeah, bass pedal. Uh-huh. And you just leave it like that? That's all.
I don't ever tighten, I don't ever un-tighten. If it rain on it, I take the rag and I wipe it off good and that's it.

Well, nice. When you're not playing it, Alec, do you plug it in once in a while? No. You just leave it a little light itself. What about your snare drum? You say you have a light in your snare drum? I have a light in my snare drum. And when do you use that light? I use my foot this and all of it. I use that. Oh, I see. Just when you're playing, but when you're not playing you don't bother with it. Yeah, I do. That looks very nice. What are you turning your snare drum? You got to bring it up. Now what note?

Is there any particular note? That's OBC. Boy, that? Turn it up. Great. That's all your traps. Your big Chinese symbol is about 16 inches. Yeah. Yeah. I see this. That drum is almost. Boom. Yeah. We're going to have a hard zoom. We got a double card here for that. Yeah, we. Oh, here. Yeah, that she is. We're going to have a hard zoom. Yeah, we. Oh, here. Yeah, that she is. Wait a while. You want to take the other one now? I know the two of them combine and mix up together. Yeah, this is it. You just plug it. My glove might be loose. Well, it might be loose or burn up. Yeah, sometimes. You have to take the head off then to get it, huh? Yeah, that's your glove. That's all it is. That's all it is. That's all it is. That's all it is. Yeah, that's all it is. That's all it is. That's all it is. Yeah, this is it. Yeah, this is it. You just plug it. My belt might be loose. You have to take the head off then to get it. Yeah, that's one here. That's one here.
I like to look at the snaps on that. I like them doing that.

That's about a 14 inch drum and about a 6 inch, I guess. 6 inch pearl shell. That's Ludwig too, is it? Yeah. We have a job of fixing up some snares on a drum we have too. In the old days, there the light went on. The light went on then. Yeah. Nice light. The bulb is loose. You have to lean it over the right way.
Yeah, that's great. What have you got in here, Allie? What's this here? Right here. Right here. Oh, this is this here. That's for tum tum, two effects.
Oh, tum tum effect. Oh, yeah. That tum tum effect, tight effect. Either way. Most drums don't have that. Oh, I see. Take a really long like that. Yep.
Different kind of effect you want. That's a nice drum set. Any of these symbols, did you carry on the parades with you?
Well, no. That's a symbol, what we had. That's the Christ symbol, huh? In other words, give me an idea about what I'm talking about. See, that tum effect. Mm-hmm .

That's the sizzle, I call it a sizzle symbol sometimes, don't they? Right, right. It's like little rivets in there, isn't it? Yeah. Yeah, about a dozen, there are about eight little rivets in there. That's the turn. Let's see what make that is. That's a nice Turkish one, sounds good. I was wondering if it's one of the ziljins. I don't use a sizzle, do I have it? Abanis sent me a sock signal, Turkish signal. Boy, what happened about the sock signal? And I played at the American Legion Hall. Oh, somebody else at the door. I had a sock signal when I went back that night. Someone stole it. Oh. Where? The American Legion Hall down here on Royal? Royal Street. Mm-hmm. And they stole all my symbols. Went to the police and all, never did part. Was anybody much used in the old days? Did they use the sock symbol very much? When did that come out? In the old days, never did they use the sock symbol. You didn't even know what sock symbol was. You see, you're up. That wood block reminds me of that's rather just a small... Yeah. About the...
That one's an eighties I built.

Seven inch block. You only use one cowbell now, do you? Yes, sir. About a five inch cowbell. Five inch cowbell. Got them mounted right on the same stand. That's a nice drum set. Do you know anybody that has one of those old pedals anymore? Where we could find anybody that might have one of those old... No, I would like to borrow. A lot of people I know would like to have one. I'd like to borrow. Really.
You think you'd use it again, Allie?

No, I wouldn't use it again, but I'd just keep it. Yeah. The old keepsake, I'd like to have one. Yeah. But I'm going to see a guy, and if I do... I'll let you know, Mr. Russell. If you find an extra one, I wouldn't want to take one of you... One of yourself, but sometimes... If you find one where I could buy one, I'd sure be glad to get one too. You have everything in two cases. Your base drum and everything else goes in one case then, does it? I'm at a job, I'm supposed to play tonight, I don't know. I never went to the guy yet, they're supposed to get it. I don't know where it's on me, I think. There's a Chinese symbol over there, too.
How often do you work nowadays?

Well, sometimes twice a week, sometimes once a week. Sometimes once a week, huh? It's been slow though, since Carnival's been slow. It's been slow since Carnival. You can work once a week nowadays, you're doing well. I'll tell you one thing. I see them drummers just about that high, and I can't sit that high and play golf or nothing. I was going to ask about that. I got sick, I got sick, high. And that's it. I can't go, I see some colors stand up. They almost stand up to play the big. I can't do it. I tried. I even bought them one of those chairs.
What do you have there, a little seat, a folding seat in there, do you like? Just a pillow.
You sit on an ordinary chair like that. I have a chair with a pillow. With that little pillow. I see. And I never get tired of my legs.
You never do. I just want to say, when you use your leg for beating, do you take your action from your ankle or from your whole leg?

You leave your heel down on the floor and just from your ankle, your toe. Some fellas stomp the whole leg from the hip, you know. Well, I guess it's all how you start off. Yeah, I think they get more tired doing that than just your ankle. Yeah. I really, if I get tired, I really give a single beat until my leg gets rested and I start back in a double beat. Uh-huh. Yeah. That's a good idea. I was going to ask on the parades, in the old days, where did the drummers, where did they march in the parade? Were they at the very back of the band or in the middle or somewhere? Well, they were at the back of the band. It was only later they started. I noticed the Eureka band uses the trumpets in the back. Well, I tell you though, Mr. Russell, I really think it's better. I think it's better. In the middle. In the middle. You know, that's hard in the back.
You have to beat louder, you mean?

No, it's just that the time is harder for you to, you know, get all the instruments together. You have to hear them, hear all of them. The vibrations, when they do boop, that thing's gone, that sound is gone.
Yeah, it goes up ahead.

Yeah, but see, when you're in the middle like that, you can more sort of have that time to work in just like a clock. Probably easier to hear it. I think so. I think it's better. The way they got it now. But that was a string before. Well, the Eureka is the only one that uses it. The other fellas still do it the old way, I think. I was going to ask too, I know Natty Dominic, you told me a long time ago, they used to always start out with the right foot. When they go one, two, one, two, in marching, the right foot would go back. But in the army bands, they all start at the left foot. That's what I was taught, I was taught in the left foot. You were always taught in the left foot. Before the war, First World War. I see, if you start at your right foot, you're going to make a wrong step. But you take the left foot to start at. And just the same way you're making them rolls. That's what I learned when I was learning how to make a roll. Drop a stick, drop a stick, drop a stick, drop a stick, start at your left hand. And you get the method, the method shows you the left hand. Yeah, I've seen those methods too. You've seen it. And you start like that. And you increase. That push, you know you're making a roll. Oh, oh, oh, oh, see? And just the way with your left foot. In marching, your left foot is the same. Don't swear.
You say you were taught to beat with your foot. Were you taught to beat with your left or your right foot when you were learning? Right foot, right foot. I'm right, I'm right hand and right foot.
Right foot. My left hand probably could beat with that foot to your left hand.
But I guess you could, you could, like with a sock symbol, you could use in your left foot.
The left foot is your sock symbol.
Did you, the time that you used your sock symbols, how did you like it? Well, I, I, it was hard when I first started.
But I, I think it's wonderful. Because it helps to balance the time.
Otherwise you've got something for both legs. You see, it's like, you play along. See that? That keeps the time.

See. That keeps the time. See. That keeps the time with that. Yeah. That comes in on the after beat. Come on after beat. That's the time. Got you. You can't go nowhere. comes in on the after beat. Come on after beat. You can't go nowhere.
You don't find that tiring? Huh? You don't find that to be tiring? No.

I mean you could use it, but just like anything. But I mean I think it's one of them socks in. Because if you start a certain tempo, you're going to keep that tempo. And they can't get away from it. Keep that tempo. You got that hook there working with this hook. Ain't nobody going to run away from it. I tell them go ahead and run.
Well where do you use it? Do you use it all through the piece or just whenever you... All through the piece.

All through. Not unless you're playing like a tiger rag or something like that. I mean that you're going to... You see a different sub song you get there you play that socks in where you work your socks in. Where you get tiger rag or them scarp-jarp numbers or something like that. You're going to... Your work is that box, that little box there. That snapper. That's where you're going to work. And you ain't going to work no double four. You're going to work single beat. Because you can't make all that with that. Because they ain't going to sound like nothing. It's not giving no effect to the music. If you play... If you play a double beat on the numbers like this, well it don't give no effect to the music. You play tiger rag and you play with a double beat. And they don't give no effect if you're drumming on the snare drum. That's right. Because that's what is driving what you're making on the snare drum. Yeah, yeah. But... A lot of fellas don't play with it. Why? Because I know why.
I'm going to tell you why. Because there's nothing down there. Can't make no roll.
Anything sound... I ain't a drummer. Anybody can make noise, but not anybody can't play a drummer.
Would you have any advice for anybody learning a drum now, Alex? Any young boy or anything like that?

Well... The advice that I think about a drummer... is learning music... and learning the effect of music... instead of playing something that you don't know what you're playing. But not to copy behind nobody else. Have your own ideas. That's what makes a drummer. Now, you making something... and I come back and don't make a single thing. Well, they're tired of hearing you. You go here... This band, this band... got an arrangement. He sold me an arrangement. I got a band. You got a band. Now, you want something you're arranging. People come to hear me in a band. They hear that arrangement. You play that arrangement. Come to hear me. I'm not... I'm nowhere. But if you play one type of drum and I play another type of drum, one of us is going to sound the best.
Yeah.

Somebody's going to fall to one of us. Yeah. But if you playing the same thing I'm playing, that don't sound like nothing. Yeah. Music is a funny thing. People think that music is just a... Oh, I don't know. Well, I'm a musician. Oh, I don't know. Anybody can play music. Anybody can play music. I'm going to tell you what my grandma used to say. That's music. No musician. And musician. In French they say musician. And in English they say music. So that's two meanings. No. No. Not everybody that carries a drum is a drummer. No. No. No. No. No. And you catch that amongst the best of musicians. Because some tell you man I'm this and I'm that and I'm that and I'm this. Oh wow. And when you come to five he's nowhere. You catch some fella he might feature me in the number. After that number he's lost. He ain't nowhere.
Yeah. He just knows what number's on.

Now when I was working down here at the Melody Inn. We had a little combo down there. Saxophone player that played with me down there. Sunday. Harold Dajon. Harold Dajon was on sax. Same piano player was there with me playing. Simon Fraser.
Yeah.
Not Simon Fraser. That was a cousin or something like that. Smitty. Smitty. I can't think he was last name. The one that was that Sunday. And had a fella by the name of Lionel Favos playing trumpet.
That guitar player huh wasn't it? Huh? Wasn't that guitar player too? No.
George Daniel started over there with me.
Oh yeah.

I was about to say. But then some kind of humbug George Daniel and the man had a George Quick. So I had to get him a piano player. So I got him a piano player. And we used to play all kind of type of music. So one night, I hope I know you might have seen Ed Butterson around there. He's a rock and roll. Mr. Boo. Oh I heard of him. He was a Betty Boo. Freddie Boo or Betty Boo. I don't know anyway. He came down there. Him and his drummer. Well, he asked. The piano player could he play a number. Told him yeah. Drum player said, Oh, let's see then. Well, for the kind of type of music they played amongst them two. You understand the idea. Just them two that rock and roll stuff. After they got you to play piano. This fellow booed. People would clap for him. Well, just then. One of those women came and asked for a number. I forget just about what number it was anyway. It was a Dixieland number and then we played all kind of type of music down there. We played a little rock and roll down there. So piano player told him to sit in. Go ahead. Play that. You can sit in with the band. A while I go take a smoke. Drum player he wanted to get us. No, sit down there. I said. If you want to answer, go ahead. You were talking about some job down for the rock and roll. Was that place called High Del? High Del. Down around the clay bank. I remember. High Del's play. So we let them play. And Spinner and I went to take a smoke on the outside. And when we came back he said, ah, come on man. Say yeah. See. We can't play that type of music. And I looked at him and I said, well you support being a musician. You support being a musician. I said, you ought to be able to play any kind of type of music if you're a musician. But see that a lot of rock and roll stuff, that's nothing but the, I don't know what to call it. I think it stinks. If you want to know the truth about it. I can't see no rock and roll music because to me the horns are not tuned. They don't sound like they're in tune to me. And to play rock and roll music, you got to have a good singer. And you got to have a fire play guitar and clown. Now if you got that you got that. But that's what the people crazy about. I mean the younger generation come today. But for it when they come down to musician you can't call a new musician. Now without, without knocking a man or without trying to flick my head fat down with no. Man made a fortune. Yeah. But what does he got? What does he got? Outside one boy in that band, because that's the get-off man. Outside that disco band. Yeah. And George Dino was always talking about him, that he doesn't know one chord from another, but he's making a million dollars. He don't know a chord, he don't know a chord, he don't know a chord, but two keys. Outside of that he's lost. He's got something that people want so I guess this. But he got what the public want. Yeah, so yeah. He made a fortune. Yeah. Well anytime you tell him to sit in a band, he can't sit in a band. No he doesn't. And what is rock and roll? Rock and roll with one beat. It's a one beat number. Yeah. Well I was going to ask about that old cymbal when you had the little cymbal fastened to the foot pedal. And it always hit, every time you hit the bass drum. Every time you hit the bass drum, it had a little, something like a piece of metal. Yeah I remember those things. It would hit that ching, ching, ching. So it was always on the beat, not the after beat with that. No, no, always on the beat. Now I wondered in the parade bands, the bass drummer now hits on the beat of the bass drum and the cymbal after the cymbal. So boom, boom, boom, right. That's right. In the old days, did they ever hit like they did on that bass drum and the pedal at the same time with the cymbal together? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Did they ever hit the cymbal? See that point? Yeah. The cymbal and the bass drum together somehow. Yeah. That's what I wondered. Now they usually hit it after. Yeah, one after beat, yeah. Mostly in the old band, they started like that. Both the bass drum and the cymbal, the hands right together. Yeah, yeah. But then your snare drum, when you had that cymbal there, you'd come in on after beats. That's right. On your big cymbal on your snare drum. That's right.
I was wondering how that worked. I'd just like one more question. Something that struck my mind a little earlier, you were talking about the San Suu Ksi Hall.
San Suu Ksi Hall.
Usually I've heard that pronounced San Suu. Is that the correct pronunciation? San Suu Ksi. San Suu Ksi.
S-O-U-C-I-C-I. San Suu Ksi Hall.
You sing a sign, haven't you, Ralph? Yeah, but I've usually heard it pronounced San Suu. I thought it was French.

I was going to ask you, when you were a boy, did you learn French? Did you mention your grandmother spoke French? She did. I could talk a little, not much. My grandmother was strictly French. I thought maybe the whole family spoke French when you were a boy. Well, yeah, most of the whole family would talk. Yeah, but I, I mean, I could talk it pretty good. I could understand it pretty good. But I never kept it a... You went to a regular public school. Oh, yeah. I wondered, was your family Catholic? Catholic. They were all Catholic, raised. Yeah, all Catholic. Yeah. Thought you might have gone, some of the schools might have been French at that time or something like that. Well, my, she went to French school. Yeah. My grandmother, that's all she spoke. She couldn't understand English. She couldn't, you couldn't understand what she was saying sometimes. The one that died, the one that raised Bonnie. Yes. Now, do you have anything else you wanted to add? If not, but we don't want to bother you all day. You may have to work yet tonight. Well, there's nothing that I want to add. But, like I say, to be a good drummer, the most essential thing, the essential thing in a drummer is his time. You can be whatever so good drummer you want to be, but if you haven't got your time, you know that. That's one thing that a professor always taught me. Time. And a little quotation, time don't waste for no one. So, that's all that I'm able to tell you. Well, we certainly enjoyed the interview and talking to you, and we really learned a lot about those old times. Well, I appreciate very much all of the time you've taken. Anything that can help you out here? I'd be too glad to give it to you. Well, thank you very much, and we'll turn her off. Thank you very much for being here. Thank you for being here.

segments.title: Opening: name, date and place of interview
segments.summary: Bigard gives his full name, spelling of his nickname, and the date (30 April 1960) at his home on St. Peter.

segments.title: Birth in the Creole part of New Orleans and musical family
segments.summary: Born 1899 on Villere Street in the French part of town; heard Dixieland; his uncle Emile Bigard played violin, brother Barney and cousin Natty Dominique played music.

segments.title: Uncle Emile Bigard's bands, West End Bungalow
segments.summary: Personnel of the West End Bungalow band with the uncle on violin and the other bands he played in, including Sidney Desvignes, King Oliver and Kid Ory.

segments.title: First job at Tom Anderson's with the Duconge brothers; drum sound
segments.summary: Bigard started on drums, had lessons with Cantrell, and had his first job at Tom Anderson's cabaret with the Duconge brothers; he talks about his Ludwig drums and old-time melodic drumming.

segments.title: Tom Anderson's neighborhood; father's clarinet and starting drum lessons
segments.summary: He describes Anderson's on Rampart and the Annex, and tells how his father bought a clarinet but he skipped clarinet lessons to learn drums on a pad.

segments.title: Cantrell's method, strictness and Perron band personnel
segments.summary: Lessons used Carl Fischer's method; Cantrell was strict, sent him to sub in Perron's band, whose members are named, and taught strict time and footwork.

segments.chapter: Brass band and the Lyric Theater
segments.title: Carrying drums, streetcar permits and Excelsior Brass Band
segments.summary: He doesn't regret ignoring his father's advice; recalls getting streetcar permits for drums and playing parades and funerals with the Excelsior Brass Band.

segments.chapter: Brass band and the Lyric Theater
segments.title: Excelsior Brass Band personnel and snare and cymbal setup
segments.summary: Members of the Excelsior band under Na-Na Moret, its size, and how he played snare drum with a cymbal on the side while another man played bass drum.

segments.chapter: Brass band and the Lyric Theater
segments.title: The Lyric Theater band under John Robichaux and Midnight Rambles
segments.summary: The Lyric band played jazz for vaudeville shows, led by Professor Robichaux; he describes the theater, rehearsals, Midnight Rambles and late dances.

segments.chapter: Brass band and the Lyric Theater
segments.title: John Robichaux band personnel
segments.summary: Names the musicians in Robichaux's band, including Harrison Barnes, Willie Pajeaud, Charlie McCurdy and Sam Dutrey Sr.

segments.title: Barney Bigard learning clarinet; violin in old Dixieland; the one-beat style
segments.summary: A long account of how Barney learned from Papa Tio and Lorenzo Tio, swapped lessons with Albert Nicholas, went to Chicago and joined Duke Ellington; also how violinists played and why Dixieland is a one-beat music.

segments.title: Dixieland versus ragtime versus jazz
segments.summary: They discuss two-beat versus four-beat playing, what Dixieland and ragtime meant, and why today's bands are not playing real Dixieland.

segments.title: Duconge band repertoire and arrangements
segments.summary: The Duconge band played Dixieland, read stock orchestra arrangements they bought, and faked afterward.

segments.title: When the word jazz began; uncle's death and Barney's whereabouts
segments.summary: Jazz was used after World War I; uncle died at 49; Barney's grandmother raised him and he is back on the road with Louis Armstrong.

segments.title: Getting Barney started in Oh Man Bernard's orchestra
segments.summary: Bigard got Barney his start in a small band rehearsing by St. Bernard Market and recalls its members.

segments.title: What became of the Duconge brothers
segments.summary: One brother is reportedly in Europe, another became a policeman in St. Louis, and Adolphe was killed in a car accident.

segments.title: Playing with Buddy Petit's band
segments.summary: Bigard played about three years with Buddy Petit, whose band is named and who was in such demand he took nine jobs a night.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's playing, repertoire and Kid Rene
segments.summary: Petit played cornet by ear, drank hard, played Scott Joplin-type numbers, and rivalled Kid Rene, whose reputation rose above Armstrong's locally.

segments.title: Drum set on the advertising trucks
segments.summary: The drum set he used on the trucks had an overhead foot pedal, one cymbal and a woodblock, and he sat at the front of the truck.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's illness and death across the lake
segments.summary: Petit lost his health to tuberculosis across Lake Pontchartrain and died there; Bigard only played jobs with him there.

segments.title: Kid Rene's trumpet and the Brown Derby; battle of the bands on trucks
segments.summary: Kid Rene played high above the staff and later worked with Bigard at the Brown Derby; bands used to buck against each other on the streets.

segments.title: Not imitating other drummers; his own toughness
segments.summary: He never copied other drummers, only listened and practiced his own ideas, and says he was tough in his day.

segments.title: Working with Sidney Desvignes and the Maple Leaf band
segments.summary: After Petit he played about two years with Desvignes's orchestra in town, and separately worked with the Maple Leaf band including on the steamer Capitol.

segments.title: Desvignes's orchestra and reading drum parts
segments.summary: Desvignes led a reading orchestra, which meant drum parts, unlike the small faking bands.

segments.title: Cantrell's lessons: fees, practice, rolls and strictness
segments.summary: Lessons twice weekly at fifty cents; two hours' practice daily; nine months on the pad before the drum, mostly rolls; Cantrell was strict.

segments.title: Professor Mineta, the Havana trip and the Martell family band
segments.summary: He credits Professor Mineta with teaching him, tells of missing a Havana job and touring with the Martell family band, with Mineta as leader.

segments.title: Uncle's trade at home and Bunk Johnson at his rehearsals
segments.summary: His uncle made cigars at the family shop at 1726 North Villere; Bunk Johnson came to rehearsals at his house, where Bigard watched as a boy.

segments.title: Being fired from the Maple Leaf band and replaced by Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: A long story of watching Henry Martin, playing with Bob Lyons, and being fired by the Maple Leaf band for Barbarin and then asked back.

segments.title: Uptown versus downtown bands and Bob Lyons's band
segments.summary: Uptown bands faked more, downtown was more musically trained; he describes Bob Lyons's band, its jobs and personnel.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: King Oliver and Kid Ory at Economy Hall and National Park; brother Barney's early bands
segments.summary: Where he heard Oliver and Ory play dances, and Barney's early work with Amos White and when he started.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Barney's name and the old clarinet
segments.summary: Questions on Barney's real name and what happened to the family clarinet.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Kid Rene at the Cadillac nightclub
segments.summary: After leaving gambling work he returned to music with Kid Rene at the Cadillac, where Papa Kutcher begged him to stay.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Five years at the West End bungalow
segments.summary: After Desvignes, Bob Lyons and the Maple Leaf he joined Walter Decou's four-piece band at the bungalow for about five years.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Original Maple Leaf Band personnel
segments.summary: Names the original Maple Leaf Band: Camilla Todd on piano, the Gaspers, Willie Bontemps and himself.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Playing with Chris Kelly, the Blues King
segments.summary: About three or four years in Chris Kelly's band, whose members are named and which played mostly blues.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Drumming for the blues
segments.summary: Blues needs slow tempo, a single bass drum beat and snare rolls; the roll is the essential skill of a drummer.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: First recording and singing in the band
segments.summary: He never recorded in those days and did not sing; band members might sing along.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Livening up the band and playing with feeling
segments.summary: Drummers shout to encourage the band; blues needs feeling and snare work rather than tom-toms.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: What made Chris Kelly's band stand out on the blues
segments.summary: Kelly played plunger-muted trumpet on Kelly's Love and the band had no printed arrangements.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Best orchestras and the Scott Joplin repertoire
segments.summary: He ranks Celestin, Desvignes, Maple Leaf, Robichaux and Tuxedo among the true orchestras.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Quadrilles and waltzes: orchestras versus jazz bands
segments.summary: Jazz bands like Kelly's did not play quadrilles; only the orchestras did.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Travel limits and the Black and Tan after Chris Kelly
segments.summary: With Kelly he stayed near home, then played the Black and Tan with Professor Mineta, Henry Martin and others.

segments.chapter: Kid Rene, Chris Kelly and the bungalow
segments.title: Maple Leaf excursions and Fate Marable's band
segments.summary: The Maple Leaf band played excursions across the lake while Marable's orchestra, with Baby Dodds, played the other boat.

segments.title: Light in the bass drum and never retuning heads
segments.summary: He keeps a light in the bass drum to keep the head dry and tight, and never broke a head on a drum he had for years.

segments.title: Showing the drum set: lights, tuning and pearl snare
segments.summary: They look at the lights in his bass and snare drums, tuning pitch, the Ludwig snare and the sizzle cymbal.

segments.title: Stolen cymbals, sock cymbal and an old pedal
segments.summary: His cymbals were stolen at the American Legion Hall; he talks about cowbell, wood block and wanting an old foot pedal.

segments.title: Working now and drumming seated
segments.summary: He works once or twice a week and sits low on a chair with a pillow.

segments.title: Foot technique, parade drummer positions and marching left foot
segments.summary: He plays from the ankle; in the old days drummers marched at the back; marching starts on the left foot like rolls.

segments.title: Using the sock cymbal and single versus double beat
segments.summary: He praises the sock cymbal for keeping time and explains when to play single beat on the bass drum, as on Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Advice to young drummers
segments.summary: Learn music, have your own ideas, don't copy, and not everyone who carries a drum is a drummer.

segments.title: Melody Inn combo and rock and roll
segments.summary: He recalls his combo at the Melody Inn, a rock and roll drummer sitting in, his dislike of rock and roll, and the old cymbal pedal.

segments.title: Pronunciation of Sans Souci Hall
segments.summary: They settle how to spell and say Sans Souci Hall.

segments.title: French-speaking family; closing remarks on time
segments.summary: His grandmother spoke only French and the family was Catholic; he closes saying a drummer's most essential thing is time.
